newsitem.title: USA: Simpson lawyer hammers at police credibility.
newsitem.headline: Simpson lawyer hammers at police credibility.

text.p: O.J. Simpson's defence attorney hammered away at police credibility on Wednesday, suggesting at the ex-football star's civil trial that there was a code of silence among officers.

Robert Baker also contended that police investigating the murders of Simpson's ex-wife and a waiter friend may have agreed on a version of events after allegations they had planted evidence to frame Simpson.

Baker's questioning prompted several testy exchanges with patrolman Daniel Gonzalez over what he wrote in his official report after the June 12, 1994 murders of Nicole Brown Simpson and Ronald Goldman and what a detective attributed to Gonzalez in an interview six months later.
Gonzalez grew increasingly frustrated at Baker's sarcasm and at one point snapped at the lawyer: "Do you understand what I am trying to tell you?"

The uniformed Los Angeles policeman was at the murder scene and at Simpson's nearby estate the morning the bodies were discovered. Simpson was acquitted last year of murder, but is being sued in civil court by the victims' families.

During the criminal trial, the defence sought to show Simpson was framed and that some evidence may have been planted. Baker has been pressing the same line in his questioning of police officers, detectives, criminalists and expert forensic witnesses.

Pointing out several discrepancies between officer Gonzalez' official report after the murders and an interview the patrolman gave to Detective Ron Phillips in Jan. 1995, Baker asked Gonzalez if there was a "code of ethics to cover up other police officers?"
"Yes, you get promoted for burning each other," Gonzalez shot back.
Baker then asked him if he had been promoted, and the six- year veteran officer replied: "You have to work in interal affairs before you become a captain. That should explain something to you."
"I don't consider my rank a promotion," Gonzalez said testily, adding "I answered your question."

Baker, trying to show that police may have agreed on a version of events, asked Gonzalez why he had not mentioned in his official report seeing blood spots inside Simpson's Ford Bronco the morning after the murders, yet Det. Phillips' notes on their interview, said he did.
"I saw blood in the Bronco," Gonazalez said, exasperatedly stressing each word slowly.

The lawyer also pointed out that Gonzalez made no mention of petting Nicole Brown Simpson's dog tied to a post near the crime scene with bloody paws in his report, and yet, according to Phillips' notes, the officer said he played with the Akita.
Baker also asked Gonzalez about the actions of detectives, including Mark Fuhrman, at Simpson's estate the morning after the bodies were discovered outside Nicole Brown Simpson's nearby condominium.

Gonzalez said he saw two of the detectives take Simpson's grown daughter, Arnelle, out to see her father's Bronco parked at the curb. That account conflicts with the testimony of the detectives and will further fuel the defence attack on their credibility.

Gonzalez said Fuhrman, branded a racist who planted a bloody glove on Simpson's property by the criminal defence team, had climbed over the fence of Simpson's estate, but he did not know who ordered the detective to do that.
